column1: What are Ground Control’s main responsibilities?
column2: Taxi instructions to/from the duty runway; obtain/relay IFR clearances if Clearance Delivery is unavailable; provide weather information.

column1: Does Clearance Delivery have a control function?
column2: No — it is used solely for the delivery of IFR clearances.

column1: What does the Tower control and issue?
column2: Controls runway traffic and airborne traffic in the control area; issues takeoff and landing clearances; provides airport advisory info to arriving flights if ATIS is absent.

column1: What does Departure Control do?
column2: Ensures separation between departures; sequences/separates IFR and participating VFR; provides radar service including VFR assistance.

column1: What is ARTCC’s role regarding IFR clearances?
column2: Central authority for issuing IFR clearances; also issues route assignments, provides traffic separation, issues NOTAMs, and provides current weather as required.

column1: What does Approach Control handle?
column2: Controls all IFR aircraft from ARTCC to tower; radar separation/sequencing for IFR and assists VFR; provides arrival information on initial contact.

column1: FSS common frequencies and primary purpose?
column2: Primarily civilian services (military may use); common freqs 122.2 and 255.4. Also flight plans, ARTCC relay, lost-aircraft assist, PIREPs.

column1: List the normal elements of an IFR clearance.
column2: Aircraft ID; clearance limit; departure instructions or SID; route; altitude; departure frequency; IFF code; any holding instructions; other info as required.

column1: Training-command vs real-world clearance readback?
column2: Training: read back all clearances verbatim. Real world: must read back runway assignment and hold-short instructions; read back deviations from filed to show acceptance; may refuse unacceptable clearances; precede readbacks with call sign.

column1: When must you report entering or leaving holding?
column2: Always, except: military terminal, radar contact, instrument training.

column1: When must you report leveling at a new altitude?
column2: Need not report unless in RVSM airspace (FL290–FL410).

column1: Lost communications — what IFF/transponder code and Guard freqs?
column2: Squawk 7600 under all weather conditions. Guard: 243.0 and 121.5. Also try other/previous frequencies; ATC will use Guard and NAVAID freqs.

column1: Primary objective of lost-communications procedures?
column2: Preclude extended IFR operation in the ATC system in VMC; land as soon as practicable.

column1: VMC lost-comms actions and light-signal acknowledgments?
column2: Maintain VMC and land ASAP (not at unsuitable/unauthorized fields or minutes short of dest). Use VFR cruising altitudes if possible (E odd / W even+500). Rock wings (day) or flash lights (night) to acknowledge tower light signals.

column1: What does AVEFAME mean for IMC lost communications?
column2: Continue flight using AVEFAME: determine correct route (AVEF), altitude (AME — highest), and time to leave the clearance limit.

column1: Lost-comms route priority (AVEF)?
column2: A = Assigned in last clearance; V = if Vectored, direct to fix/airway in clearance; E = Expected further routing; F = Filed flight-plan route.

column1: WARNING about clearance to an intermediate point off your filed route?
column2: Do not accept a clearance to an intermediate point not on your filed route and short of destination without first obtaining expected further routing.

column1: Lost-comms altitude — fly the highest of which (AME)?
column2: A = altitude Assigned in last clearance; M = Minimum IFR altitude (MEA, MOCA, ESA, MSA, OROCA); E = Expected altitude from ATC.

column1: When do you leave a clearance limit that IS a fix from which an approach begins?
column2: Commence descent/approach as close as possible to EFC if received; otherwise as close as possible to ETA (T/O + ETE).

column1: When do you leave a clearance limit that is NOT a fix from which an approach begins?
column2: Leave at EFC if received; otherwise upon arrival over the clearance limit.

column1: In-flight emergency — transponder code and distress vs urgency call?
column2: Squawk 7700. Distress: MAYDAY (slide: “MAY, MAY, MAYDAY”); Urgency: PAN-PAN ×3. Then station, ID/type, nature, weather, intentions, position/heading, altitude, fuel, souls on board, other useful info.

column1: What mnemonic covers IMC lost-comms route + altitude selection?
column2: AVEF (route) + AME (altitude) → AVEFAME; fly highest of A/M/E for each route segment.
